content: Sambucus nigra, commonly referred to as Elder or Elderberry, is a species of elder native to most regions of Europe, northwest Africa, and southwest Asia. It is also known by other names such as Black Elder, European Elder, European Elderberry, European Black Elderberry, Common Elder, or Elder Bush, particularly when distinguishing it from other species within the Sambucus genus. This plant thrives in a variety of environmental conditions, including both wet and dry soils, and it prefers sunny locations. Sambucus nigra is a deciduous shrub that typically grows to a height of 4 to 6 meters, although it can occasionally reach up to 10 meters. They are pinnate in structure, consisting of five to seven (rarely nine) leaflets. Each leaflet is 5 to 12 centimeters long and 3 to 5 centimeters wide, with serrated edges. The plant produces hermaphroditic flowers during mid-summer, which are grouped in large corymbs measuring 10 to 25 centimeters in diameter. The individual flowers are white, approximately 5 to 6 millimeters in diameter, and have five petals. These flowers are primarily pollinated by flies. The fruit of the plant is a dark purple to black berry, measuring 3 to 5 millimeters in diameter, and it grows in drooping clusters during late autumn. These berries serve as a vital food source for many fruit-eating bird species, particularly Blackcaps. Sambucus nigra is closely related to several other species native to Asia and North America, which are often considered subspecies of Sambucus nigra by some botanists. Sambucus nigra has a variety of uses, both medicinal and ornamental. However, it is also classified as a poisonous plant for mammals and is sometimes regarded as a weed. The flowerheads of the plant are commonly used to make infusions, which are popular as refreshing beverages in Northern Europe and the Balkans. These infusions are commercially available as elderflower cordial and similar products. The berries of the plant are edible but only after cooking, as all other parts of the plant contain toxic calcium oxalate crystals and are considered poisonous. Historically, the strong-smelling foliage of Sambucus nigra was tied to the manes of horses to repel flies during riding. Various parts of the plant, including the stem bark, leaves, flowers, fruits, and root extracts, have been used in traditional medicine to treat conditions such as bronchitis, cough, upper respiratory tract infections, and fever. In Beerse, Belgium, the berries are used to produce a type of Jenever known as Beers Vlierke. For further information, references include Flora Europaea, the ITIS database, the USDA PLANTS Database, and the Germplasm Resources Information Network.
